subtopics.title: Geography and Basic Facts
subtopics.summary: The Aravalli range is the oldest mountain system in India, about 2 billion years old and dating to the Precambrian era. It extends 692 km from Champaner in Gujarat through Rajasthan and Haryana to Delhi. Its highest peak is Guru Shikhar, at 1722 m, near Mount Abu in Rajasthan.
facts: Oldest mountain system in India, about 2 billion years old
Dates to the Precambrian era
Extends 692 km from Champaner (Gujarat) to Delhi
Passes through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi
Ends at Raisina Hill in Delhi
Highest peak: Guru Shikhar, 1722 m
Guru Shikhar is near Mount Abu in Rajasthan
Source of rivers including Luni, Banas and Sabarmati
Mineral base: copper, zinc, lead, silver and Makrana marble
Boasts 22 wildlife sanctuaries, four tiger reserves and bird parks

subtopics.title: Ecological Services of the Range
subtopics.summary: The range works as a natural barrier that slows the eastward spread of the Thar Desert by blocking dust-laden desert winds. It deflects moisture-laden monsoon winds eastward, shields northern plains from cold, dry winter winds from Central Asia, and filters pollution for Delhi-NCR. Its fractured, weathered rocks let rainwater infiltrate and recharge aquifers in semi-arid regions.
facts: Natural Great Green Wall: barrier against eastward spread of the Thar Desert
Blocks dust-laden desert winds
Monsoon modulator: deflects moisture-laden winds eastward toward the Indo-Gangetic Plains
Aids rainfall distribution in North India
Winter climate shield against cold, dry winds from Central Asia
Forested stretches absorb carbon dioxide in Delhi-NCR
Forested stretches trap PM2.5 and improve air quality
Highly fractured and weathered rocks enable rainwater infiltration
Recharges aquifers in semi-arid Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat
Habitat for over 300 plant species and 120 bird and animal species

subtopics.title: Mining Curbs and the 2025 Supreme Court Ruling
subtopics.summary: Protection measures began with 1990s mining restrictions and continued through Supreme Court orders, including a 2009 blanket mining ban in parts of Haryana and a 2024 order barring fresh leases. In 2025 the Court accepted a uniform scientific definition of an Aravalli hill, based on an MoEF&CC expert committee. The Forest Survey of India assessment found that over 90 per cent of the Aravalli landscape would be excluded under the 100 m threshold, which sparked fears of more mining and construction.
facts: 1990s: restrictions on mining
2009: SC blanket mining ban in parts of Haryana
MC Mehta vs Union of India: mining restricted and banned across large parts of the range
2024: SC order bars fresh leases; Central Empowered Committee tasked with scientific review
2025 definition based on MoEF&CC Expert Committee
Aravalli hill: landform rising 100 m or more above its immediate local terrain
Aravalli ranges: clusters of such hills within 500 m, including intervening areas
Mining banned in core/inviolate areas such as protected areas, ESZs, wetlands and tiger reserves
Freeze on new mining leases until a Management Plan for Sustainable Mining is prepared by the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education
Over 90% of Aravalli landscape excluded by the 100 m threshold

subtopics.title: Aravalli Green Wall and Afforestation Policies
subtopics.summary: The Aravalli Green Wall Project, inspired by Africa's Great Green Wall, is a 1400 km by 5 km ecological corridor across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi, launched in 2019. It targets restoring 1.1 million hectares by 2027 through native plantations, around 1,000 nurseries and removal of invasive species. Wider national policies include the National Forest Policy's one-third target, the National Mission for a Green India, CAMPA and India's Bonn Challenge pledge.
facts: 1400 km x 5 km ecological corridor across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi
Covers 29 districts
Target: restore 1.1 million hectares by 2027
Launched in 2019; nodal ministry is the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Works: native plantations, around 1,000 nurseries, invasive species removal, water body restoration
National Forest Policy (1988): at least one-third of land under forest/tree cover
National Mission for a Green India is part of the National Action Plan on Climate Change
CAMPA uses funds collected from diverted forest land for afforestation
Bonn Challenge: India aims to restore 26 million hectares by 2030
Matri Van Initiative: 750-acre urban forest under 'Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam'

quizzes.passage: The Aravalli range is one of the oldest mountain systems in India. It runs through Gujarat, Rajasthan and Haryana, and reaches Delhi. The range acts as a natural barrier that slows the spread of the Thar Desert, because it blocks dust-laden desert winds. It also influences the southwest monsoon by guiding moisture-laden winds towards the Indo-Gangetic Plains. In winter, its hills shield the northern plains from cold, dry winds. Its forested stretches help clean the air of the National Capital Region by absorbing carbon dioxide and trapping fine particles. Its forests are also home to many plant and animal species. Rocks in the range allow rainwater to seep into the ground, which supports groundwater in semi-arid areas. The area also supports mining-based livelihoods and industries. Because of these uses, the range has faced pressure from mining and urban growth for many years. Courts and government bodies have therefore introduced several measures to limit mining and restore forests. In 2025, the Supreme Court accepted a uniform scientific definition of an Aravalli hill, based on an expert committee's advice. The definition determines which landforms receive protection, and it has raised concern that mining and construction could expand into areas left outside it. Understanding both the ecology and the legal steps helps explain why the range is in the news.

quizzes.passage: Restoring degraded land has become a central goal in the Aravalli region, where mining and urban growth have put pressure on the landscape for decades. Planners have drawn inspiration from a large African project that aims to hold back the spread of desert. The approach focuses on planting native species on land that has lost its vegetation, which helps hold soil and supports local wildlife. Nurseries are set up to grow saplings for continuing planting drives, so that seedlings are ready when they are needed. Damaged water bodies are also being restored, because healthy ponds and lakes help recharge groundwater. Invasive plant species, which crowd out native plants, are removed so that the native forest can recover. The work is coordinated centrally but depends on many partners, including non-governmental organisations, private companies and local communities. Government policy has treated afforestation as a long-term commitment rather than a one-time campaign. The restoration is meant to control desertification, improve air quality and strengthen climate resilience in the Delhi-NCR region. Together, these measures aim to protect the region's green cover and water supply. The nurseries and planting drives span the states that the corridor crosses, including Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Delhi. Plantation work covers degraded land, and the approach relies on species that grow naturally in the region.
